title: Design a News Feed
summary: A full framework walkthrough of a social feed: fan-out on write vs read, the celebrity problem and the hybrid fix, feed storage sizing, cursor pagination, and a ranking pipeline.

questions.prompt: Explain **fan-out on write** and **fan-out on read** for a news feed. Which makes reading faster, and which makes posting cheaper?
questions.hint: When does the copying into each follower's feed happen?
keyPoints: Fan-out on write (push): when a post is created, its ID is inserted into every follower's precomputed feed
Fan-out on read (pull): at read time, fetch recent posts from everyone the user follows and merge them
Push makes reads fast (one lookup) but costs N writes per post for N followers
Pull makes posting cheap (one write) but reads are slow and expensive (query all followees)
questions.answer:
- **Fan-out on write (push):** when someone posts, workers look up their followers and **insert the post ID into every follower's precomputed feed** (e.g. a Redis list per user). Reading is then **one lookup**: fast and cheap. But a post costs **N writes for N followers**: 300 followers means 300 inserts, and a celebrity with 80M followers means 80M.
- **Fan-out on read (pull):** a post is written **once** to the author's own timeline. When a user opens their feed, the service fetches recent posts from **everyone they follow** and merges them. Posting is cheap, but reading is slow and expensive: following 300 accounts means 300 lookups plus a merge on every feed open.

So **push makes reading faster**, and **pull makes posting cheaper**. Since feeds are read far more often than people post, most systems push for normal users and pull only for celebrities (the hybrid).

questions.prompt: A social app has **50M DAU**. Each user posts **2 times/day** on average, has **300 followers** on average, and opens the feed **15 times/day**. Estimate average post QPS, feed-read QPS, and fan-out inserts per second with pure push. Then size the feed cache if each user's cached feed holds **800 post IDs** of 8 bytes.
questions.hint: Use 86,400 s/day (≈ 10^5 for a quick check).
keyPoints: Fan-out inserts: 1,160 × 300 ≈ 350,000/s
Feed cache: 50M × 800 × 8 bytes = 320 GB (before overhead and replication), so a sharded cache cluster
questions.answer: Posts `1e8/86,400 ≈ 1,160/s`; reads `7.5e8/86,400 ≈ 8,700/s`; fan-out `1,160 × 300 ≈ 350k inserts/s`; cache `5e7 × 800 × 8 B = 3.2e11 B = 320 GB` (more with overhead and replicas) → sharded Redis by user_id.

questions.prompt: Your feed uses fan-out on write. A pop star with **80 million followers** posts, and suddenly posts from regular users take **15 minutes** to show up in feeds. Explain what happened and how you'd redesign.
questions.hint: What is sitting in front of the regular users' fan-out jobs in the queue?
keyPoints: One post generated 80M feed inserts, which swamped the fan-out workers and queue (a backlog delaying everyone else)
Hybrid: don't fan out posts from accounts above a follower threshold; followers pull those posts at read time and merge them
Cache celebrities' recent posts heavily since many feeds will pull them
Optionally separate queues/priorities so large fan-outs can't starve normal ones, and skip fan-out to inactive users
questions.answer:
**What happened:** with pure fan-out on write, that one post created **80 million feed inserts**. They all went into the same fan-out queue, ahead of everyone else's posts. If the workers manage, say, 100,000 inserts/s, that's 80M ÷ 100k = **800 s ≈ 13 minutes** of backlog. Regular users' posts sat in line behind it, hence the 15-minute delay. (And many of those 80M followers weren't even online.)

**Redesign: a hybrid.**
- Set a **follower threshold** (e.g. 10k–100k). Accounts above it **don't fan out**. Their posts stay in their own timeline.
- At read time, the feed service fetches the recent posts of the few celebrities the user follows and **merges** them with the pushed feed (merge k sorted lists by post ID).
- **Cache celebrities' recent posts** heavily: millions of feeds pull the same short lists, so serve them from a replicated cache.
- **Separate queues or priorities** for big fan-outs, so a large job can't starve normal posts.
- **Skip fan-out to inactive users** (e.g. not seen in 30 days) and rebuild their feed by pulling when they return.

Now a celebrity post is one write, and normal posts appear in seconds again.

questions.prompt: Write `mergeFeeds(lists, cursor, limit)` where `lists` is an array of arrays of post IDs, each sorted **newest first** (bigger ID = newer). Return up to `limit` IDs that are **older than** `cursor` (strictly smaller), newest first, plus the `nextCursor`.
questions.hint: Keep one pointer per list; repeatedly take the largest current head that's below the cursor.
keyPoints: Skips IDs >= cursor in each list
Repeatedly picks the largest head among the lists (or uses a max-heap) and advances that list's pointer
Stops at limit or when all lists are exhausted
nextCursor is the last ID returned (or null if none)
States complexity: O(limit × k) with a scan, O(limit × log k) with a heap

questions.prompt: Why should a feed API use **cursor-based pagination** instead of `?page=2&size=20`? And why does the feed cache store **post IDs** rather than full post objects?
questions.hint: What happens to page 2 when three new posts arrive while you're reading page 1? What happens when a post is edited?
keyPoints: With offsets, new posts at the top shift items down, so the user sees duplicates or skips posts
A cursor (e.g. "older than post ID X") stays stable as new posts arrive, and is efficient to query
Storing IDs keeps each feed small (8 bytes per entry vs ~1 KB per post), so the cache is far cheaper
Post content is stored once and hydrated at read time, so edits, deletes and like counts are always current
questions.answer:
**Cursors vs offsets.** With `?page=2&size=20`, the server skips the first 20 items. Feeds change constantly: if 3 new posts arrive while you read page 1, everything shifts down by 3, so page 2 starts with the last 3 posts you already saw (**duplicates**). Deletions shift things the other way, so you **skip** posts. Offsets are also slow: `OFFSET 1000` still walks past 1,000 rows.

A **cursor** says "posts older than post ID X" (`?cursor=940&limit=20`). New posts at the top don't affect what's older than 940, so pages stay **stable**, and with time-sortable IDs it's an efficient indexed range query.

**IDs vs full posts in the cache.**
- **Size:** an ID is **8 bytes**; a post with text and metadata is ~**1 KB**. For 50M users × 800 entries, that's 320 GB of IDs vs ~40 TB of copied posts: over 100x cheaper.
- **Freshness:** the post is stored **once** and **hydrated** (fetched) at read time from a post cache. Edits, deletes and like counts are always current, instead of being stale copies in millions of feeds that you'd have to chase down and update.

questions.prompt: Product wants to switch the feed from chronological to **ranked** ("most relevant first"). Design the ranking flow within a **200 ms** feed latency budget. What data do you need, and how does pagination change?
questions.hint: You can't score millions of posts per request. Where do candidates come from?
keyPoints: Candidate generation: gather a bounded set (hundreds to a few thousand) of recent post IDs from the pushed feed plus pulled celebrity posts
Features: author-reader affinity, engagement counts, post age (time decay), content type; precomputed and cached so lookups are fast
Scoring with a formula or ML model, then re-ranking for diversity and filtering deleted, blocked or already-seen posts
Latency budget split across steps, with batched feature fetches and a fallback to chronological order if ranking times out
Pagination: rank once per session and page through the stored ranked list (or exclude seen IDs), since scores change between requests
questions.answer:
**1. Candidate generation (~20 ms):** you can't score millions of posts per request. Gather a bounded set, a few hundred to ~2,000 recent post IDs, from the user's **pushed feed** plus **pulled celebrity posts** (the same lists the chronological feed uses).

**2. Feature fetch (~40 ms):** for each candidate, look up **precomputed** features in a fast store, in **batched** requests:
- author–reader **affinity** (how often they interact),
- **engagement** counts (likes, comments, shares),
- **post age**, for time decay,
- content type (photo, video, link).

**3. Scoring (~50 ms):** a formula (e.g. affinity × engagement ÷ (age + 2)^1.5) or an ML model scores every candidate.

**4. Re-ranking and filtering (~20 ms):** drop deleted, blocked or **already-seen** posts; add **diversity** (not five posts in a row from one author).

**5. Hydrate the top 20 and return (~40 ms)**, leaving headroom within the **200 ms** budget. If ranking times out, **fall back to chronological** order rather than failing.

**Pagination changes:** scores change between requests (new likes, time decay), so an ID cursor no longer works. Instead, **rank once per session**, store the ordered list of IDs (e.g. in Redis for 30 minutes), and return a cursor that is a position in that saved list. Alternatively, re-rank on each page but **exclude IDs already shown**.
